clue.text: Sportspeople seeing injuries including leaderless crew, flailing rowers

indicators.note: with no leader, the word loses the letter at its front
to include something is to take it inside, so one set of letters wraps around the rest

parts.note: welts are raised marks on the skin from a blow

indicators.note: flailing limbs thrash about wildly, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: the word with its first letter removed
an eight is a rowing crew of eight oarsmen

explanation.surface: A rowing team, flailing badly, ends up covered in cuts and bruises.
explanation.walkthrough: WELTS opens to take in ERW (the shuffled REW) followed by EIGHT, giving WELT-ERW-EIGHT-S. 'Crew' looks like the rowing word, but the rowing crew is clued by 'rowers'.
explanation.definitionFit: Welterweights are boxers or wrestlers competing in a particular weight class, so they are sportsmen and women.

clue.text: Amusing Western, A Horse Is Hot

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for west or western
taken as written
gee-gee, a childish word for a horse
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A film critic praising a comic cowboy movie called 'A Horse Is Hot'.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make 'A Horse Is Hot' look like a film title, and 'Western' like its genre; each word is really a separate piece. GG (gee-gee) is a crossword staple for horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Waggish describes someone playfully humorous, like a wag or joker, so it is a synonym for funny.

clue.text: Composer's catalogue in the auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is where an audience listens, so we go by what is heard rather than written

parts.note: a catalogue is a list

explanation.surface: A concert-goer reading a composer's list of works while seated in the hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composer's' reads as possessive, but the 's is 'is': the composer is the catalogue, when heard. Franz Liszt's name is said exactly like 'list'.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Liszt was a celebrated Hungarian pianist and writer of Romantic music, an example of the category.

clue.text: Delivering 'second-to-last' finales

indicators.note: read as an instruction, 'S to last' sends the leading letter round to the end

parts.note: sending something is delivering it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Second-to-last' looks like penultimate, but it splits as S (second) to last: the S at the front of SENDING moves to the end. S is the standard abbreviation for second.
explanation.definitionFit: Endings and finales are both the concluding parts of a show, piece of music or story.

clue.text: Poor tenant was wont to be thrifty

definitions.note: the answer is a proverb urging thrift, not a verb phrase

indicators.note: something poor is in bad shape, so these letters are in a sorry state and need rearranging

parts.note: the fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A hard-up renter who has always been careful with money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' looks like part of 'to be thrifty', but it belongs to the anagram letters; the definition is just 'be thrifty'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb advises that if you never squander anything you will never go short, which is the essence of frugal living.

clue.text: Very old (50), soldier heads north to find accommodation there

indicators.note: in a down entry, going north means travelling up the column, so the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: so means very, as in 'so tired'
O is a standard abbreviation for old
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
a GI is an American enlisted soldier

explanation.surface: An elderly fifty-year-old soldier marches up to the Arctic looking for somewhere to stay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very old' looks like one phrase but splits into two pieces, and the bracketed 50 is a Roman numeral. 'There' points back to 'north', so the definition leans on the wordplay's direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Igloos are dome-shaped snow-block shelters built by Inuit people, the archetypal dwellings of the frozen Arctic.

clue.text: Those on the Corinthian omnibus?

parts.note: surface reading: passengers riding a bus in the Greek city of Corinth
setter's reading: omnibus is Latin for 'for all', and Corinthian means Greek, so it is the Greek phrase for everybody, the many

explanation.surface: Commuters riding a bus around ancient Corinth.
explanation.walkthrough: A bus was originally an omnibus, Latin for 'for all'; the answer is a Greek phrase meaning 'the many', so it is the Greek word for all comers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek-derived phrase means the common people or the masses, everybody in general rather than an elite.

clue.text: Like ABBA? Like a turnip?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: from Sweden, as the pop group was
second meaning: swede-ish, resembling a swede

explanation.walkthrough: A swede is the British name for the root vegetable Americans call rutabaga, a kind of turnip; the second reading splits the answer as SWEDE-ISH.
explanation.definitionFit: The band came from Sweden, so is Scandinavian by nationality; a turnip-like root resembles a swede in a playful coinage.

clue.text: Wise men heading off for a long time

indicators.note: with the head taken off, the front letter of the word goes

parts.note: sages are wise men

explanation.surface: The Magi set off on a lengthy journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading off' reads as setting out on a journey, but it means removing the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: 'For ages' is an informal idiom for a very lengthy period, so the plural noun stands for it.

clue.text: Renunciation of stinking acrid slime

indicators.note: something stinking is rotten, and rotten letters fall apart into a new order

parts.note: the ten letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone disowning a foul-smelling, sharp-scented ooze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stinking' sits naturally beside 'acrid slime' as a description, which hides its job as the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A disclaimer is a formal statement denying responsibility or giving up a claim, which is a renouncing.

clue.text: Single knitted item? Beguiled? Not originally

indicators.note: without what it had originally, the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: to be smitten is to be charmed or beguiled

explanation.surface: Someone charmed by a lone piece of knitwear, wondering if they were ever really captivated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single' matters: mittens come in pairs, so one item is the singular form.
explanation.definitionFit: A mitten is a hand covering often made of wool on needles, and one of a pair is a single piece.

clue.text: Cheap Italian novelist with no means to be heard

parts.note: Umberto Eco, author of The Name of the Rose
taken as written
a mic (microphone) is a device for making a voice heard

explanation.surface: A budget Italian author who cannot afford to make himself heard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No means' reads as poverty, but 'no' stands alone and 'means to be heard' is the microphone.
explanation.definitionFit: Economic can mean inexpensive or offering good value for money, as in an economic price.

clue.text: Digitally alter, very quietly, attractive 'outsize' host — not half, that's accepted

indicators.note: dropping half a word leaves only part of it, here the front two letters
what is accepted is taken in, so the outer letters wrap around the others

parts.note: pianissimo, the musical marking for very soft
hot means sexually attractive
OS is the abbreviation for outsize, as on clothing
the first half of the four letters

explanation.surface: A glamorous, oversized presenter quietly airbrushed for a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: PP (pianissimo) takes in HOT, OS and HO, giving P-HOTOSHO-P.
explanation.definitionFit: The image-editing software has become a verb for retouching pictures by computer, a trademark used generically.

clue.text: Subsequently, the Scripture lessons at university in progress

parts.note: taken as written
RE is religious education, the British school subject
in British usage a student is 'up' at Oxford or Cambridge
something on is happening, under way

explanation.surface: Later on, a theology student's Bible classes at college are under way.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is Religious Education, a subject in British schools; 'up' for being at university is a British idiom, as is 'come down' for leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: Thereupon is a formal adverb meaning immediately after that, so it means afterwards or next in time.

clue.text: A little busy, the French hotel; nothing to write home about

indicators.note: only a small part of the word is wanted, its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word
la is French for the (feminine)
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A fairly lively French hotel that was nevertheless unremarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A little busy' reads as 'somewhat crowded' but it takes just one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Blah as an adjective means dull or unexciting, and 'nothing to write home about' is an idiom for mediocre.

clue.text: Witnesses hijack, reportedly

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: to hijack a plane is to seize it

explanation.surface: Bystanders observe a hijacking, according to news reports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Witnesses' looks like a noun, people in court; it is the verb, matching the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To witness an event is to observe it with your own eyes, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Little singer to squabble repeatedly

parts.note: to spar is to argue or bicker
the same idea given a second time, another word for a quarrel

explanation.surface: A small vocalist prone to constant bickering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repeatedly' asks for the squabble twice, using two different words: one that rhymes with car and one that rhymes with cow.
explanation.definitionFit: A sparrow is a small songbird, and birds that sing are commonly called singers in crosswords.

clue.text: Extremely professorial tenor, most insipid

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for tenor
weedy means feeble or lacking character

explanation.surface: A highly academic singer who is also extremely dull.
explanation.walkthrough: Tweedy describes the stereotypical academic in a tweed jacket; 'extremely' supplies the superlative ending.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweedy means having the old-fashioned bookish manner of a lecturer dressed in woollen jackets, so the superlative is most academic-looking.

clue.text: Everyman's flipping furious in far-off land?

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: the setter refers to himself, me
irate means very angry

explanation.surface: The setter declares himself absolutely livid while abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping furious' reads as British slang for very angry; 'flipping' is the reversal signal and the 's is 'is'. The question mark admits the definition is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: An emirate is a state ruled by an emir, such as those in the Gulf, distant countries from a British view.

clue.text: Heartfelt lines describing fine uniform following small change

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so the outer letters go around the inner ones

parts.note: a sou was a low-value French coin
L for line, doubled for the plural
F is the pencil-grading abbreviation for fine
U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Moving verses about a smart uniform, written after a slight alteration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' means drawing round, as in geometry. 'Following' puts the coin first; a sou was an old French coin of little value, a byword for small change.
explanation.definitionFit: Soulful means expressing deep emotion, so it is a synonym for sincere and deeply felt.

clue.text: Believed unpleasant smell that's disgusting lost at last

parts.note: BO is body odour
ugh is what you say at something disgusting

indicators.note: at the very end, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A foul odour was thought to have finally gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's disgusting' is the exclamation UGH, the noise itself rather than a description.
explanation.definitionFit: To buy a story is the informal idiom for accepting it as true, so the past tense means credited.

clue.text: A cop went to resort city on Atlantic

indicators.note: read as re-sort, the letters are sorted again into another order

parts.note: the eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A police officer went on holiday to a seaside town by the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like a holiday destination, but read as re-sort it signals rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Cape Town is South Africa's legislative capital, lying on the Atlantic coast near the Cape of Good Hope.

clue.text: Some vicar, uselessly tragic figure

indicators.note: only some of the letters are wanted, a run lying inside the words

parts.note: a run of letters crossing the comma

explanation.surface: A clergyman so ineffectual that he cuts a pitiful figure.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma and the word break are ignored when reading the letters through.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Icarus flew too near the sun on wax wings and fell to his death, a classic doomed character.

clue.text: African capital city reaching Atlantic, for starters?

definitions.text: African capital city reaching Atlantic, for starters?

indicators.note: starters come at the beginning of a meal, so the opening letters are taken

parts.note: the first letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A capital city in Africa that stretches to the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: the first letters spell a city which is itself an African capital on the Atlantic.
explanation.definitionFit: Accra is the capital of Ghana, sitting on the Gulf of Guinea, an arm of the Atlantic Ocean.

clue.text: A grandpa ('Pop'), shortly tipsy, offering misinformation

indicators.note: cut short, the word loses its final letter
a tipsy person staggers about, so the letters lurch into another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: A slightly drunk grandfather spreading fake news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' in brackets looks like the grandpa's nickname, but it is part of the letters, trimmed to PO before the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Propaganda is biased or misleading material spread to promote a cause, so it is a form of deliberately false information.

clue.text: Somewhat shamefaced, keeling over where drinks are served

indicators.note: a ship keeling over capsizes and turns upside down, so the letters run backwards
only to some extent, so just a part of the word is wanted

parts.note: a run of four letters near the end of the word

explanation.surface: A sheepish, unsteady customer falling over in a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeling over' fits a drunk in a bar, which disguises it as the backwards signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A cafe is a small restaurant or coffee shop serving hot beverages and light refreshments.

clue.text: What the King's men did: failed

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in the nursery rhyme, all the king's men rushed to where Humpty Dumpty fell off his perch
second meaning: an idiom for a business collapsing

explanation.walkthrough: In 'Humpty Dumpty', the egg sat on a wall and fell, and all the king's horses and men came to it; the literal reading meets the idiom for going under.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for a firm or person being ruined or going bankrupt, so it means collapsed.
